author: Diptanu Choudhury
text: We are seeing backlash against sandboxes for primarily a couple of reasons - vendors don't support users to overcommit compute. You can't pay for N cores and overcommit the number of sandboxes that are run on those cores. In reality agents don't uniformly use resources during [quote: Arlan on code hallucinations & data freshness]
suggestedEngagement: Agree and add nuance: agent workloads are fundamentally bursty — unlike always-on services, they spike hard then go idle, so overcommit is the natural fit. Ask how they think vendors should price it.
Share experience: at scale you can colocate agent runs that have different burst profiles to smooth out utilization — curious if tensorlake is pursuing that approach.
Challenge/extend: vendors may resist overcommit because of noisy-neighbor risk on CPU-intensive sandboxes — how does diptanu think about isolation guarantees when you overcommit?

author: Victor Taelin
text: My final thoughts on Opus 4.6: why this model is so good, why I underestimated it, and why I'm so obsessed about Mythos. When I first tested GPT 5.4 vs Opus 4.6 — both launched at roughly the same time — I was initially convinced that GPT 5.4 was vastly superior, because it did [things Opus couldn't]. After extended testing, I've completely reversed that take.
suggestedEngagement: Ask what specific agentic tasks changed his mind — code architecture, multi-step reasoning, or something else? Shows genuine curiosity and invites a substantive thread.

Connect the Mythos obsession to the enterprise security angle: if Opus 4.6 is the model and Mythos shows where capability goes next, what does that mean for enterprise deployment risk? The model that writes perfect code can also find perfect exploits.

Add the harness layer angle: the model selection debate matters less than the harness governance layer for enterprise deployments — does his take on Opus 4.6's strengths change what harness capabilities you actually need at scale?
